summary: For ages 7–9: coral reefs are built by colonies of tiny living ANIMALS called polyps (the hard reef is the limestone skeleton they build — made by living animals, not just lifeless rock, and not a plant); reefs are among the most biodiverse marine habitats; and they are called 'rainforests of the sea' because of both their variety of life and their role as a living structure that shelters countless other species. The counter-intuitive 'coral is alive — it's an animal' fact is the key surprise; the biodiversity is the wonder. Keep bleaching/threats light at this stage.
misconceptions: 'Coral is a rock / a stone' — not knowing the reef is built by living animals (only the limestone skeleton is hard).
'Coral is a plant' — misled by its branching, flower-like, rooted appearance.
'A reef is one big creature' — rather than a colony of many tiny polyps (and a whole community).
'Reefs are colourful decorations' — missing that they are the most biodiverse marine habitat and shelter for countless species.
Taking 'rainforests of the sea' as being about greenery/plants rather than about biodiversity and structure.

activities.title: Zoom from reef to a single living polyp
steps: Start with a view of a whole busy reef, then step inward: reef → one branch of coral → a single polyp with its ring of tentacles and a mouth.
Name what you see at the smallest scale: a tiny living animal, not a rock or a stone.
State in your own words how billions of these tiny animals, each building a hard limestone cup around itself, add up to the giant reef structure over long time.
Explain what tells you a polyp is an animal and not a plant (it has a mouth and catches drifting food with stinging tentacles; seaweed has no mouth or tentacles and makes its food from sunlight).
activities.insight: The hard reef is the limestone skeleton that colonies of tiny living animals (polyps) build; coral is an animal, not a rock or a plant.

activities.title: Count the species: reef versus bare seabed
steps: Explore one reef scene and tap or point to each different creature; keep a running tally of how many distinct species you can spot.
Do the same count on a bare patch of seabed and compare the two tallies.
Say in a sentence what the contrast shows about how much variety of life a small reef area holds.
activities.insight: Reefs are among the most biodiverse habitats in the ocean — a tiny area holds a huge variety of life, felt most strongly by contrast with a barer habitat.

activities.title: Unpack the 'rainforests of the sea' analogy
steps: Look at a side-by-side comparison of a reef and a rainforest.
List two reasons the names match: (a) exceptional variety of life, and (b) both are physical living structures that provide homes and food for everything else.
Explain why the nickname is NOT mainly about colour or greenery/plants.
activities.insight: The analogy captures biodiversity AND the reef as a living structure that shelters other species — like a forest provides homes for forest animals.

activities.title: Grow a reef over time (optional dynamic model)
steps: Seed a few polyps and watch (or step through) as they divide and secrete limestone, building structure over time.
Watch a species counter climb as the growing structure attracts more animals.
Say how this shows that tiny builders make a giant structure, and that a larger, more complex structure tends to provide homes for more kinds of animals.
activities.insight: Tiny living builders make a giant structure over long time; in this model a larger, more complex structure tends to offer more homes, so biodiversity tends to increase as the reef grows.

activities.title: Check your understanding
steps: Answer: is coral a rock, a plant, or an animal? Justify your choice.
Compare the variety of life on a reef with that on a bare seabed and say which is more biodiverse.
Explain in a sentence why reefs are called the 'rainforests of the sea'.
activities.insight: Learners can state and justify all three core ideas: polyp-is-an-animal, reef biodiversity, and the analogy.

activities.title: Meet a talking coral polyp (optional spark)
steps: Interview a polyp character (or a reef biologist) who explains in role: 'I'm an animal!', how its colony built the reef over a long time, and how it catches food while staying fixed in one place, using its moving tentacles.
Ask your own wonder questions and compare the answers to what you learned from the zoom and counting activities.
activities.insight: A polyp's first-person account can make the 'it's alive and it's an animal' surprise memorable and invite curiosity.

checkQuestion: Here is a photo of a coral reef, all knobbly and colourful. I tell you a coral reef is alive — it is built by thousands of tiny animals. Is that true, and if a coral is an animal, how does it eat and grow when it never moves around like a fish does?
checkAnswer: A coral is a living thing — the hard reef is made by huge colonies of tiny animals called polyps, each like a minute sea anemone in a little cup of limestone it builds around itself. It doesn't chase food: it catches tiny drifting plankton with stinging tentacles, and (in reef-building corals) it also houses tiny algae inside its body that make food from sunlight, which is why reefs grow in shallow, sunlit, warm water. The rock is what the animals build, not the animal itself.
